resources.instruction: Challenge the scope before writing rules, and record the result in the "Scope and rationale" section of 02-spec.md. Answer briefly three questions: (1) what the system already has that solves part of this (a function, endpoint, screen, table) and whether the spec is rebuilding something that exists; (2) what the minimal change to reach the goal is, which work can be deferred without blocking the goal, and which is a wish disguised as a requirement; (3) complexity: if the work would touch more than 8 files, add more than 2 new classes or services, or need more than 3 stages, ask yourself whether the same goal can be reached with less and give a reason for each. Then choose one mode and record why for the reviewer to confirm at GATE A: KEEP (the scope is right, focus on error paths, boundary values, tests), REDUCE (move everything that does not block the goal to "out of scope") or EXPAND (only when the brainstorm or messages asked for it; mark the expansion clearly). Once chosen, keep to it: do not silently reduce or expand later. For small and obvious work (a typo, a one-line configuration) skip this step.

Cover the scenarios before fixing the acceptance criteria. Go through these dimensions, keep only those that really apply and record each one you skip with a one-line reason: kinds of user; extreme input values (empty, null, maximum length, unicode, special characters, a string of only whitespace); timing (two operations at once, retry); scale (0, 1, many elements, pagination boundaries); state transitions (first use, abandoned halfway, redo); failure chains (a slow or failing database or external service, a partial write); authorization; data integrity (duplicates, orphaned references, cascading deletes); integration (a changed contract, version skew); compliance (personal data, audit logs); business logic (a value of 0 or negative, limits). Each applicable dimension yields 3 to 5 concrete scenarios, rated Critical, High, Medium or Low (Critical: data loss or corruption, a security leak; High: broken functionality for a group of users). Scenarios rated High and above and every error path must become acceptance criteria; the rest go into "Known limitations".

Acceptance criteria quality. Each AC describes one observable behaviour (a status code, a message, the state of the data), not how to implement it. Replace vague words with concrete values ("valid" becomes 200 characters accepted, 201 characters rejected). The AC for an error path goes with the AC for the success path of the same operation. No two ACs contradict or duplicate each other; each AC is verifiable by an automated test. Check again before finishing: every business rule BR has at least one AC, and every AC leads back to a BR or a user story.
